title: Pide kıymalı
subtitle: Turkish boat-shaped flatbread with spiced lamb mince
excerpt: Pide are long, boat-shaped Turkish flatbreads baked in a hot oven with a filling of spiced lamb mince, onion, pepper, and tomato. They puff, blister, and pick up a little char at the edges while the filling bubbles. They are somewhere between a pizza and a pasty and are far more than either.
sourceNotes: Pide are the Turkish flatbread found in pide salons all over Turkey. The kıymalı (minced meat) version is one of the most popular. The boat shape is formed by rolling the dough into an oval and folding in the long edges before baking.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: The dough can be made up to 24 hours ahead and refrigerated after its first rise. The filling can be cooked a day ahead and chilled.
recipe.temperatureNote: Fan 220 C. Use the highest heat your oven can reach. A baking stone or steel helps enormously.

content.text: Pide are Turkey's answer to pizza, but the comparison sells them short. A proper pide is doughy, chewy, and scorched in exactly the right places, while the filling stays juicy and fragrant rather than drying out in the oven.

The spiced lamb filling is seasoned with Aleppo pepper, cumin, and sweet paprika then spread thinly over the raw dough so the meat cooks in the same blast of heat that browns the base. The folded-in edges hold the filling in place and give a thick, bread-like crust.

Heat is everything here. Preheat the oven as hot as it will go for at least 30 minutes. If you have a baking stone or steel, use it; if not, a very heavy baking tray preheated in the oven is a solid substitute.

Combine the flour, yeast, salt, olive oil, and warm water in a large bowl. Bring together into a soft dough, then knead for 8 minutes until smooth. Place in an oiled bowl, cover with a damp cloth, and leave in a warm place for 1 hour until doubled. Meanwhile, fry the onion and pepper in olive oil over medium heat for 8 minutes until soft. Add the lamb mince and break it up well. Cook for 5 minutes until the meat loses its pink colour. Stir in the tomato, spices, and salt and cook for 5 more minutes until the mixture is fragrant but not dry. Stir in the parsley. Set aside to cool.

Preheat the oven to its highest setting (at least 240 C / fan 220 C) with the baking trays inside for at least 30 minutes. Divide the dough into 4 pieces. On a lightly floured surface, roll each piece into a long oval about 30 cm by 15 cm. Spread a quarter of the filling over each oval, leaving a 2 cm border around the edge. Fold the long edges up and over to enclose the filling slightly and pinch the ends together to form a boat shape.

Remove the hot trays from the oven carefully and slide the pide directly onto them. Bake for 12 to 15 minutes until the base is golden and the edges have browned and blistered. Serve immediately with lemon wedges.

items.symptom: Base is soft and not crispy
items.cause: Tray not hot enough or oven not preheated long enough
items.fix: Preheat the tray for at least 30 minutes; the sizzle when the dough hits the tray is what creates the crispy base.

items.cause: Too little tomato or over-cooked filling before baking
items.fix: The filling should be moist but not wet before spreading. Use enough tomato in the filling.
Pinch the ends firmly and fold the sides in tightly before sliding onto the tray.

content.text: The cheese version (peynirli) uses feta or white cheese spread over the base with no meat. The sucuk version adds sliced Turkish sausage. For a half-and-half pide, put different fillings on each half.

The dough can be made the night before and left to rise slowly in the fridge overnight. The filling can also be made a day ahead and chilled. Assemble and bake just before serving; pide do not hold well once baked.

Pide salons are a feature of Turkish town life, dedicated shops that bake pide in wood-fired or gas ovens and sell them to eat in or take away. The kiyma version is the most common, though cheese, egg, and spinach variations are found everywhere. Pide is sold by the slice on the street and eaten whole at the table.
